newsitem.title: USA: US asks court to lift credit union expansion limit.
newsitem.headline: US asks court to lift credit union expansion limit.

text.p: The federal regulator of U.S. credit unions asked an appeals court here to lift a lower court order preventing thousands of credit unions from expanding.

National Credit Union Administration, in a motion filed late Wednesday, asked the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia to issue a temporary stay on membership limits imposed by District Court Judge Thomas Jackon in October.
Since then, "multiple occupational credit unions and members of the public have already begun to feel the deleterious impact of the order," the agency said.
"With each day, credit unions turn away new members, lose capital invetsments and damage their relationships with sponsoring employers," the agency said.

Judge Jackson's order, arising out of a six year legal battle between credit unions and the banks, prohibited credit unions from including members from more than one occupational group, as had been permitted by NCUA since 1982.
On Dec. 4, Judge Jackson also set aside new rules adopted by NCUA in November to ease the crunch on credit unions by expanding the definition of a single occupational group.

In the brief filed Wednesday, the agency argued that Jackson's order, which applied to about 3,600 credit unions nationwide, was improper because it arose out the bank's 1990 lawsuit against one institution, AT&T Family Federal Credit Union in North Carolina.

"The first time any plaintiff in the case sought to bar the addition of new members to previously approved groups was October 7, 1996...14 years after the NCUA announced its multiple group policy," the agency said. "Neither the NCUA nor the thousands of federal credit unions that it regulates were on notice that relief of this type would ever be sought."

The agency also noted that two other lower courts have approved the NCUA's 1982 policy allowing multiple occupational groups in a single credit union. And the solicitor general, on behalf of the agency, asked the Supreme Court to take up the case this term, the agency said.
"The legal viability of NCUA's multiple group policy remains a serious and live issue," the agency said.
American Bankers Association, the lead plaintiff in the case, was not immediately available for comment. The association has previously opposed moves to reinstate the multiple group policy.
